qa.name: Iliopsoas
qa.origin: Psoas Major: transverse processes and bodies of T12–L5 vertebrae. Iliacus: iliac fossa and ala of sacrum
qa.insertion: Lesser trochanter of the femur via a shared tendon
qa.innervation: Psoas Major: anterior rami of L1–L3. Iliacus: femoral nerve (L2, L3)
qa.function: Powerful flexion of the hip; assists lateral rotation of the thigh; psoas major also flexes the lumbar spine when femur is fixed
qa.blood_supply: Iliolumbar artery; medial circumflex femoral artery
qa.clinical_note: Iliopsoas is the combined muscle formed by Psoas Major and Iliacus — individually covered in Abdomen — Posterior Wall. It is the most powerful hip flexor in the body. The femoral nerve passes between the two components in the femoral triangle. A psoas abscess tracks along the psoas sheath and may present as a groin swelling — the hip is held in flexion to reduce tension and pain. Iliopsoas tightness is assessed with Thomas' test and is a common finding in anterior hip impingement and low back pain.

qa.name: Sartorius
qa.insertion: Upper medial surface of the tibia (pes anserinus — with gracilis and semitendinosus)
qa.function: Flexes, abducts, and laterally rotates the hip; flexes the knee; assists medial rotation of the tibia on the femur when knee is flexed — the cross-legged sitting position
qa.opposing_muscle: Hip adductors (for abduction); gluteus maximus (for hip flexion vs extension)
qa.clinical_note: Sartorius is the longest muscle in the body, running obliquely from ASIS to the medial tibia. Its name derives from the Latin for tailor — it produces the cross-legged sitting position used by tailors. It forms the lateral boundary of the femoral triangle (medial boundary = adductor longus; floor = iliopsoas and pectineus). It forms the roof of the adductor (Hunter's) canal in the middle third of the thigh. The pes anserinus bursa lies between its insertion and the medial collateral ligament — a common site of bursitis in osteoarthritis.

qa.name: Rectus Femoris
qa.origin: Straight head: anterior inferior iliac spine (AIIS). Reflected head: groove above acetabulum
qa.insertion: Quadriceps tendon to patella, then patellar ligament to tibial tuberosity
qa.function: Extends the knee; flexes the hip. Only quadriceps muscle to cross both the hip and knee joints
qa.opposing_muscle: Hamstrings (knee flexion); iliopsoas acts synergistically for hip flexion
qa.clinical_note: Rectus Femoris is the only quadriceps muscle that crosses both the hip and knee — making it a two-joint muscle. The four quadriceps muscles are: Rectus Femoris, Vastus Lateralis, Vastus Medialis, and Vastus Intermedius — all innervated by the femoral nerve (L2–L4) and all inserting via the quadriceps tendon. Rectus femoris avulsion fractures at the AIIS are seen in adolescent athletes during kicking sports. It is the most commonly injured quadriceps muscle in sprinting and kicking — typically at the myotendinous junction.

qa.name: Vastus Lateralis
qa.origin: Intertrochanteric line, greater trochanter, lateral lip of linea aspera, lateral intermuscular septum
qa.insertion: Lateral border of patella and quadriceps tendon; tibial tuberosity via patellar ligament
qa.innervation: Femoral nerve (L2, L3, L4); lateral division
qa.function: Extends the knee; stabilises the patella laterally
qa.opposing_muscle: Hamstrings (knee flexion); vastus medialis (balances patellar tracking)
qa.clinical_note: Vastus Lateralis is the largest of the four quadriceps muscles. It is the preferred site for intramuscular injection in infants. Its lateral pull on the patella must be balanced by Vastus Medialis Obliquus (VMO) — imbalance leads to lateral patellar maltracking and patellofemoral pain syndrome. The quadriceps group (Rectus Femoris, Vastus Lateralis, Medialis, Intermedius) all share femoral nerve innervation (L2–L4) and insert via the quadriceps tendon. Vastus Lateralis is harvested as a flap in reconstructive surgery.

qa.name: Vastus Medialis
qa.origin: Intertrochanteric line, medial lip of linea aspera, medial intermuscular septum, tendon of adductor magnus
qa.insertion: Medial border of patella and quadriceps tendon; tibial tuberosity via patellar ligament
qa.innervation: Femoral nerve (L2, L3, L4); medial division
qa.function: Extends the knee; the oblique fibers (VMO) stabilise the patella medially, preventing lateral subluxation
qa.blood_supply: Femoral artery; medial circumflex femoral artery
qa.clinical_note: Vastus Medialis Obliquus (VMO) — the oblique distal fibers of vastus medialis — is critical for patellar tracking. VMO weakness (common after knee injury or surgery) causes lateral patellar tilt and patellofemoral pain syndrome. VMO is the last part of the quadriceps to recover after knee surgery and the first to atrophy — targeted specifically in knee rehabilitation. The quadriceps (Rectus Femoris + 3 Vasti) all share femoral nerve (L2–L4) innervation. Vastus medialis is also the roof of the distal adductor canal.

qa.name: Vastus Intermedius
qa.origin: Anterior and lateral surfaces of the upper two-thirds of the femoral shaft
qa.insertion: Deep part of quadriceps tendon; tibial tuberosity via patellar ligament
qa.innervation: Femoral nerve (L2, L3, L4); deep division
qa.function: Extends the knee; lies deep to rectus femoris and is the deepest of the four quadriceps
qa.blood_supply: Lateral circumflex femoral artery; femoral artery
qa.clinical_note: Vastus Intermedius is the deepest quadriceps muscle, lying directly on the femoral shaft deep to rectus femoris. It is the most difficult to identify separately on dissection and imaging. The articularis genu is a small muscle deep to vastus intermedius that retracts the suprapatellar bursa during knee extension. The quadriceps group (Rectus Femoris + Vastus Lateralis + Vastus Medialis + Vastus Intermedius) all insert via the quadriceps tendon into the patella, then via the patellar ligament to the tibial tuberosity — all innervated by the femoral nerve (L2–L4).

qa.name: Pectineus
qa.origin: Pecten pubis (pectineal line of pubis) and pubic tubercle
qa.insertion: Pectineal line of the femur (between lesser trochanter and linea aspera)
qa.innervation: Femoral nerve (L2, L3); may also receive a branch from the obturator nerve
qa.function: Adducts and flexes the hip; assists medial rotation
qa.opposing_muscle: Gluteus medius and minimus (abduction); gluteus maximus (extension)
qa.blood_supply: Medial circumflex femoral artery; obturator artery
qa.clinical_note: Pectineus forms the floor of the femoral triangle medially (iliopsoas forms the lateral floor). It has a dual innervation — primarily femoral nerve but sometimes also obturator nerve — making it transitional between the anterior and medial compartments. It is the most anterior of the adductor group. The femoral triangle is bounded by: inguinal ligament (superiorly), sartorius (laterally), adductor longus (medially); its floor is formed by iliopsoas and pectineus. Contents from lateral to medial: femoral nerve, artery, vein, lymphatics (NAVAL).
